raw: CHAPTER IV. The Preparation
en: [Chapter 4] The Preparation

raw: When the mail got successfully to Dover, in the course of the forenoon, the head drawer at the Royal George Hotel opened the coach-door as his custom was.
en: When the mail coach finally arrived in Dover later that morning, the chief waiter at the Royal George Hotel opened the coach door as usual.

raw: He did it with some flourish of ceremony, for a mail journey from London in winter was an achievement to congratulate an adventurous traveller upon.
en: He did so with quite a bit of ceremony, for traveling by mail coach from London in the winter was a major accomplishment that called for congratulating any adventurous traveler.

raw: By that time, there was only one adventurous traveller left be congratulated: for the two others had been set down at their respective roadside destinations.
en: By then, there was only one adventurous traveler left to congratulate: the other two had already been dropped off at their destinations along the way.

raw: The mildewy inside of the coach, with its damp and dirty straw, its disagreeable smell, and its obscurity, was rather like a larger dog-kennel.
en: The musty interior of the coach, with its damp, dirty straw, unpleasant smell, and dark atmosphere, looked a lot like a large dog kennel.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry, the passenger, shaking himself out of it in chains of straw, a tangle of shaggy wrapper, flapping hat, and muddy legs, was rather like a larger sort of dog.
en: Lorry shook himself free of the straw. He was wrapped in a messy coat, with a floppy hat and muddy legs. He looked rather like a large dog stepping out of his kennel.

raw: “There will be a packet to Calais, tomorrow, drawer?”
en: "Will there be a ferry to Calais tomorrow, waiter?"

raw: “Yes, sir, if the weather holds and the wind sets tolerable fair.
en: "Yes, sir, if the weather stays good and the wind is fair.

raw: The tide will serve pretty nicely at about two in the afternoon, sir.
en: The tide will be perfect around two in the afternoon, sir.

raw: Bed, sir?”
en: Would you like a room, sir?"

raw: “I shall not go to bed till night; but I want a bedroom, and a barber.”
en: "I won't go to bed until tonight; but I need a bedroom and a barber."

raw: “And then breakfast, sir?
en: "And then breakfast, sir?

raw: Yes, sir.
en: Yes, sir.

raw: That way, sir, if you please.
en: Right this way, please.

raw: Show Concord!
en: Show the gentleman to the Concord room!

raw: Gentleman’s valise and hot water to Concord.
en: Carry his bag and hot water to Concord.

raw: Pull off gentleman’s boots in Concord. (You will find a fine sea-coal fire, sir.) Fetch barber to Concord.
en: Take off his boots in Concord. You'll find a nice coal fire there, sir. Bring the barber to Concord.

raw: Stir about there, now, for Concord!”
en: Hurry up now, get moving on Concord!"

raw: The Concord bed-chamber being always assigned to a passenger by the mail, and passengers by the mail being always heavily wrapped up from head to foot, the room had the odd interest for the establishment of the Royal George, that although but one kind of man was seen to go into it, all kinds and varieties of men came out of it.
en: The Concord bedroom was always given to mail coach passengers. Those passengers were always bundled up from head to toe when they arrived. So the room had a funny fascination for the staff of the Royal George Hotel. Only one type of traveler ever went in.

raw: Consequently, another drawer, and two porters, and several maids and the landlady, were all loitering by accident at various points of the road between the Concord and the coffee-room, when a gentleman of sixty, formally dressed in a brown suit of clothes, pretty well worn, but very well kept, with large square cuffs and large flaps to the pockets, passed along on his way to his breakfast.
en: But all sorts of different men came back out. As a result, another waiter, two porters, several maids, and the landlady all happened to be lingering in the hallway when a sixty-year-old gentleman walked past. He was formally dressed in a well-worn but very neat brown suit, with large square cuffs and big pocket flaps.

raw: The coffee-room had no other occupant, that forenoon, than the gentleman in brown.
en: The dining room had no other guests that morning except for the gentleman in brown.

raw: His breakfast-table was drawn before the fire, and as he sat, with its light shining on him, waiting for the meal, he sat so still, that he might have been sitting for his portrait.
en: His breakfast table was set in front of the fireplace. As he sat there with the firelight shining on him, waiting for his food, he sat so still that he could have been posing for a portrait.

raw: Very orderly and methodical he looked, with a hand on each knee, and a loud watch ticking a sonorous sermon under his flapped waist-coat, as though it pitted its gravity and longevity against the levity and evanescence of the brisk fire.
en: He looked very neat and systematic. He sat with a hand on each knee. Under his vest, a loud watch ticked solemnly, as if competing with the crackling fire.

raw: He had a good leg, and was a little vain of it, for his brown stockings fitted sleek and close, and were of a fine texture; his shoes and buckles, too, though plain, were trim.
en: He had good-looking legs and was quietly proud of them. His brown stockings fit smoothly and were made of fine material.

raw: He wore an odd little sleek crisp flaxen wig, setting very close to his head: which wig, it is to be presumed, was made of hair, but which looked far more as though it were spun from filaments of silk or glass.
en: His shoes and buckles were simple but neat. He wore an odd, small, tight, light-colored wig that sat very close to his head.

raw: His linen, though not of a fineness in accordance with his stockings, was as white as the tops of the waves that broke upon the neighbouring beach, or the specks of sail that glinted in the sunlight far at sea.
en: His shirt, though not as fine as his stockings, was as white as the tips of the waves crashing on the nearby beach, or the distant specks of sails shining in the sunlight.

raw: A face habitually suppressed and quieted, was still lighted up under the quaint wig by a pair of moist bright eyes that it must have cost their owner, in years gone by, some pains to drill to the composed and reserved expression of Tellson’s Bank.
en: His shirt was as white as the foam on the breaking waves outside. His face was lit up under that old-fashioned wig by a pair of bright, lively eyes.

raw: He had a healthy colour in his cheeks, and his face, though lined, bore few traces of anxiety.
en: It must have taken him years of discipline to train his face into the cold, serious expression required at Tellson's Bank.

raw: But, perhaps the confidential bachelor clerks in Tellson’s Bank were principally occupied with the cares of other people; and perhaps second-hand cares, like second-hand clothes, come easily off and on.
en: Still, he had a healthy color in his cheeks, and his face, though wrinkled, showed very few signs of worry.

raw: Completing his resemblance to a man who was sitting for his portrait, Mr.
en: Looking more than ever like someone posing for a painting, Mr.

raw: Lorry dropped off to sleep.
en: Lorry drifted off to sleep.

raw: The arrival of his breakfast roused him, and he said to the drawer, as he moved his chair to it:
en: The arrival of his breakfast woke him up, and he told the waiter as he pulled up his chair:

raw: “I wish accommodation prepared for a young lady who may come here at any time to-day.
en: "I want a room prepared for a young lady who might arrive at any time today.

raw: She may ask for Mr.
en: She may ask for Mr.

raw: Jarvis Lorry, or she may only ask for a gentleman from Tellson’s Bank.
en: Jarvis Lorry, or she might just ask for a gentleman from Tellson's Bank.

raw: Please to let me know.”
en: Please let me know when she arrives."

raw: “Yes, sir.
en: "Yes, sir.

raw: Tellson’s Bank in London, sir?”
en: Tellson's Bank in London, sir?"

raw: “Yes.”
en: "Yes."

raw: “Yes, sir.
en: "Yes, sir.

raw: We have oftentimes the honour to entertain your gentlemen in their travelling backwards and forwards betwixt London and Paris, sir.
en: We often have the honor of hosting your gentlemen as they travel back and forth between London and Paris, sir.

raw: A vast deal of travelling, sir, in Tellson and Company’s House.”
en: There's a huge amount of travel done by the staff of Tellson and Company."

raw: “Yes.
en: "Yes.

raw: We are quite a French House, as well as an English one.”
en: We are very much a French firm, as well as an English one."

raw: “Yes, sir.
en: "Yes, sir.

raw: Not much in the habit of such travelling yourself, I think, sir?”
en: You don't travel back and forth like that much yourself, I take it, sir?"

raw: “Not of late years.
en: "Not in recent years.

raw: It is fifteen years since we--since I--came last from France.”
en: It has been fifteen years since we, since I, last returned from France."

raw: “Indeed, sir?
en: "Really, sir?

raw: That was before my time here, sir.
en: That was before my time here, sir.

raw: Before our people’s time here, sir.
en: Before any of our staff worked here.

raw: The George was in other hands at that time, sir.”
en: The George Hotel was under different management back then, sir."

raw: “I believe so.”
en: "I believe so."

raw: “But I would hold a pretty wager, sir, that a House like Tellson and Company was flourishing, a matter of fifty, not to speak of fifteen years ago?”
en: "But I would bet a good amount, sir, that a company like Tellson and Company was doing very well fifty years ago, let alone fifteen?"

raw: “You might treble that, and say a hundred and fifty, yet not be far from the truth.”
en: "You could triple that and say a hundred and fifty, and still be close to the truth."

raw: “Indeed, sir!”
en: "Is that so, sir!"

raw: Rounding his mouth and both his eyes, as he stepped backward from the table, the waiter shifted his napkin from his right arm to his left, dropped into a comfortable attitude, and stood surveying the guest while he ate and drank, as from an observatory or watchtower.
en: The waiter stepped back from the table in wide-eyed surprise. He moved his napkin from his right arm to his left, stood in a relaxed posture, and watched the guest eat and drink.

raw: According to the immemorial usage of waiters in all ages.
en: It was the ancient custom of waiters everywhere.

raw: When Mr.
en: When Mr.

raw: Lorry had finished his breakfast, he went out for a stroll on the beach.
en: Lorry finished breakfast, he went out for a walk on the beach.

raw: The little narrow, crooked town of Dover hid itself away from the beach, and ran its head into the chalk cliffs, like a marine ostrich.
en: The tiny, narrow, crooked town of Dover seemed to hide from the shore, burying its head into the white chalk cliffs like a sea ostrich.

raw: The beach was a desert of heaps of sea and stones tumbling wildly about, and the sea did what it liked, and what it liked was destruction.
en: The beach was a barren waste of stones and rocks. The sea did whatever it wanted, which was mostly destruction.

raw: It thundered at the town, and thundered at the cliffs, and brought the coast down, madly.
en: It crashed against the town and thundered against the cliffs.

raw: The air among the houses was of so strong a piscatory flavour that one might have supposed sick fish went up to be dipped in it, as sick people went down to be dipped in the sea.
en: The air in the streets smelled so strongly of fish that you might have thought the sick fish came up to town to breathe it, the same way sick humans went down to bathe in the sea.

raw: A little fishing was done in the port, and a quantity of strolling about by night, and looking seaward: particularly at those times when the tide made, and was near flood.
en: There was a little fishing in the harbor, and a lot of walking around at night.

raw: Small tradesmen, who did no business whatever, sometimes unaccountably realised large fortunes, and it was remarkable that nobody in the neighbourhood could endure a lamplighter.
en: Small shopkeepers who never seemed to do any actual business somehow made huge fortunes.

raw: As the day declined into the afternoon, and the air, which had been at intervals clear enough to allow the French coast to be seen, became again charged with mist and vapour, Mr.
en: As the afternoon faded, the air, which had been clear enough at times to spot the coast of France, grew thick with mist and fog again, and Mr.

raw: Lorry’s thoughts seemed to cloud too.
en: Lorry’s thoughts seemed to cloud over as well.

raw: When it was dark, and he sat before the coffee-room fire, awaiting his dinner as he had awaited his breakfast, his mind was busily digging, digging, digging, in the live red coals.
en: When it got dark and he sat in front of the fireplace waiting for dinner, just as he had waited for breakfast, his mind was busy digging, digging, digging in the glowing red coals.

raw: A bottle of good claret after dinner does a digger in the red coals no harm, otherwise than as it has a tendency to throw him out of work.
en: A bottle of good red wine after dinner doesn't harm someone who stares into the glowing fireplace, except that it tends to make them lose focus on their thoughts.

raw: Mr.
en: Lorry had been relaxing for a long time.

raw: Lorry had been idle a long time, and had just poured out his last glassful of wine with as complete an appearance of satisfaction as is ever to be found in an elderly gentleman of a fresh complexion who has got to the end of a bottle, when a rattling of wheels came up the narrow street, and rumbled into the inn-yard.
en: He had just poured the last glass from his bottle with a look of complete satisfaction. He was about to drink it when the clatter of wheels came up the narrow street and rumbled into the inn yard.

raw: He set down his glass untouched. “This is Mam’selle!” said he.
en: He set his glass down without drinking. "This is the young lady!" he said.

raw: In a very few minutes the waiter came in to announce that Miss Manette had arrived from London, and would be happy to see the gentleman from Tellson’s.
en: A few minutes later, the waiter came in to announce that Miss Manette had arrived from London and would be happy to see the gentleman from Tellson’s.

raw: “So soon?”
en: "So soon?"

raw: Miss Manette had taken some refreshment on the road, and required none then, and was extremely anxious to see the gentleman from Tellson’s immediately, if it suited his pleasure and convenience.
en: Miss Manette had eaten on the road and didn't need anything now, and she was very eager to see the gentleman from Tellson’s right away, if it was convenient for him.

raw: The gentleman from Tellson’s had nothing left for it but to empty his glass with an air of stolid desperation, settle his odd little flaxen wig at the ears, and follow the waiter to Miss Manette’s apartment.
en: The gentleman from Tellson's finished his glass with quiet desperation, adjusted his odd little wig over his ears, and followed the waiter to Miss Manette's room.

raw: It was a large, dark room, furnished in a funereal manner with black horsehair, and loaded with heavy dark tables.
en: It was a large, dark room. The furniture was black horsehair. The tables were heavy and dark.

raw: These had been oiled and oiled, until the two tall candles on the table in the middle of the room were gloomily reflected on every leaf; as if _they_ were buried, in deep graves of black mahogany, and no light to speak of could be expected from them until they were dug out.
en: They had been polished so many times that the two tall candles in the middle of the room were reflected back darkly on every surface. The candles looked as if they were buried in deep graves of black wood, waiting to be dug out.

raw: The obscurity was so difficult to penetrate that Mr.
en: The room was so dark that Mr.

raw: Lorry, picking his way over the well-worn Turkey carpet, supposed Miss Manette to be, for the moment, in some adjacent room, until, having got past the two tall candles, he saw standing to receive him by the table between them and the fire, a young lady of not more than seventeen, in a riding-cloak, and still holding her straw travelling-hat by its ribbon in her hand.
en: Lorry, walking carefully over the worn carpet, assumed at first that Miss Manette was in another room. But as he passed the two tall candles, he saw a young lady of about seventeen standing to greet him. She wore a riding cloak and held her straw sunhat by its ribbon.

raw: As his eyes rested on a short, slight, pretty figure, a quantity of golden hair, a pair of blue eyes that met his own with an inquiring look, and a forehead with a singular capacity (remembering how young and smooth it was), of rifting and knitting itself into an expression that was not quite one of perplexity, or wonder, or alarm, or merely of a bright fixed attention, though it included all the four expressions--as his eyes rested on these things, a sudden vivid likeness passed before him, of a child whom he had held in his arms on the passage across that very Channel, one cold time, when the hail drifted heavily and the sea ran high.
en: He looked at her: short, slender, and pretty. Golden hair. Blue eyes looking at him searchingly. A smooth young forehead that had a unique way of wrinkling into a frown, not quite confusion, not quite wonder, not quite alarm, not quite deep focus, but all four at once. The moment he saw it, he remembered a child he had once carried in his arms.

raw: The likeness passed away, like a breath along the surface of the gaunt pier-glass behind her, on the frame of which, a hospital procession of negro cupids, several headless and all cripples, were offering black baskets of Dead Sea fruit to black divinities of the feminine gender--and he made his formal bow to Miss Manette.
en: It was years ago, crossing this very Channel, on a cold day when hail fell heavily and the sea was rough. The memory faded quickly. He made his formal bow to Miss Manette.

raw: “Pray take a seat, sir.” In a very clear and pleasant young voice; a little foreign in its accent, but a very little indeed.
en: "Please take a seat, sir," she said in a clear, pleasant young voice. It had a slight foreign accent, but only a very little.

raw: “I kiss your hand, miss,” said Mr.
en: "I kiss your hand, miss," said Mr.

raw: Lorry, with the manners of an earlier date, as he made his formal bow again, and took his seat.
en: Lorry, using the old-fashioned manners of his younger days, making another formal bow before sitting down.

raw: “I received a letter from the Bank, sir, yesterday, informing me that some intelligence--or discovery--”
en: "I received a letter from the bank yesterday, sir, informing me that some information, or discovery, "

raw: “The word is not material, miss; either word will do.”
en: "The exact word doesn't matter, miss; either one works."

raw: “--respecting the small property of my poor father, whom I never saw--so long dead--”
en: ", regarding the small property of my poor father, whom I never saw because he died so long ago, "

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry moved in his chair, and cast a troubled look towards the hospital procession of negro cupids.
en: Lorry shifted in his chair and looked uncomfortably at the mirror's strange carvings.

raw: As if _they_ had any help for anybody in their absurd baskets!
en: As if they had any help to offer anyone in their ridiculous baskets!

raw: “--rendered it necessary that I should go to Paris, there to communicate with a gentleman of the Bank, so good as to be despatched to Paris for the purpose.”
en: ", makes it necessary for me to go to Paris, to speak with a representative of the bank who was kind enough to be sent there for this purpose."

raw: “Myself.”
en: "That would be me."

raw: “As I was prepared to hear, sir.”
en: "So I was told, sir."

raw: She curtseyed to him (young ladies made curtseys in those days), with a pretty desire to convey to him that she felt how much older and wiser he was than she.
en: She curtsied to him, which is what young ladies did in those days, politely showing that she respected him as someone older and wiser.

raw: He made her another bow.
en: He bowed back to her again.

raw: “I replied to the Bank, sir, that as it was considered necessary, by those who know, and who are so kind as to advise me, that I should go to France, and that as I am an orphan and have no friend who could go with me, I should esteem it highly if I might be permitted to place myself, during the journey, under that worthy gentleman’s protection.
en: "I replied to the bank, sir, that since those who advise me think it necessary for me to go to France, and since I am an orphan and have no friends to go with me, I would be very grateful to travel under that gentleman's protection.

raw: The gentleman had left London, but I think a messenger was sent after him to beg the favour of his waiting for me here.”
en: The gentleman had already left London, but I believe a messenger was sent after him to ask him to wait for me here."

raw: “I was happy,” said Mr.
en: "I was happy," said Mr.

raw: Lorry, “to be entrusted with the charge.
en: Lorry, "to be given this responsibility.

raw: I shall be more happy to execute it.”
en: I will be even happier to carry it out."

raw: “Sir, I thank you indeed.
en: "Sir, thank you.

raw: I thank you very gratefully.
en: I am very grateful.

raw: It was told me by the Bank that the gentleman would explain to me the details of the business, and that I must prepare myself to find them of a surprising nature.
en: The bank told me that the gentleman would explain the details of this business to me, and that I should prepare myself for some surprising news.

raw: I have done my best to prepare myself, and I naturally have a strong and eager interest to know what they are.”
en: I have done my best to prepare, and naturally, I am very anxious to know what it is."

raw: “Naturally,” said Mr.
en: "Naturally," said Mr.

raw: Lorry. “Yes--I--”
en: Lorry. "Yes, I, "

raw: After a pause, he added, again settling the crisp flaxen wig at the ears, “It is very difficult to begin.”
en: After a pause, he adjusted his tight light wig over his ears again and said, "It is very difficult to begin."

raw: He did not begin, but, in his indecision, met her glance.
en: He didn't start right away, but hesitated and looked at her.

raw: The young forehead lifted itself into that singular expression--but it was pretty and characteristic, besides being singular--and she raised her hand, as if with an involuntary action she caught at, or stayed some passing shadow.
en: Her young forehead wrinkled in that unique way, which was pretty and characteristic of her, and she raised her hand, as if automatically trying to catch or stop a passing shadow.

raw: “Are you quite a stranger to me, sir?”
en: "Are you a complete stranger to me, sir?"

raw: “Am I not?” Mr.
en: "Aren't I?" Mr.

raw: Lorry opened his hands, and extended them outwards with an argumentative smile.
en: Lorry opened his hands and spread them with a polite smile.

raw: Between the eyebrows and just over the little feminine nose, the line of which was as delicate and fine as it was possible to be, the expression deepened itself as she took her seat thoughtfully in the chair by which she had hitherto remained standing.
en: The frown between her eyebrows and just above her delicate nose deepened as she sat down thoughtfully in the chair she had been standing next to.

raw: He watched her as she mused, and the moment she raised her eyes again, went on:
en: He watched her as she sat thinking, and the moment she looked up at him again, he continued:

raw: “In your adopted country, I presume, I cannot do better than address you as a young English lady, Miss Manette?”
en: "Since England is your adopted home, I assume I should address you as an English lady, Miss Manette?"

raw: “If you please, sir.”
en: "If you please, sir."

raw: “Miss Manette, I am a man of business.
en: "Miss Manette, I am a businessman.

raw: I have a business charge to acquit myself of.
en: I have a business task to complete.

raw: In your reception of it, don’t heed me any more than if I was a speaking machine--truly, I am not much else.
en: As you listen to it, don't think of me as anything more than a talking machine, really, I'm not much else.

raw: I will, with your leave, relate to you, miss, the story of one of our customers.”
en: With your permission, I will tell you the story of one of our clients."

raw: “Story!”
en: "A story?"

raw: He seemed wilfully to mistake the word she had repeated, when he added, in a hurry, “Yes, customers; in the banking business we usually call our connection our customers.
en: He pretended to misunderstand why she repeated the word, adding quickly, "Yes, a client. In banking, we usually call our contacts our clients.

raw: He was a French gentleman; a scientific gentleman; a man of great acquirements--a Doctor.”
en: He was a French gentleman, a man of science, highly educated, a Doctor."

raw: “Not of Beauvais?”
en: "Not from Beauvais?"

raw: “Why, yes, of Beauvais.
en: "Why, yes, from Beauvais.

raw: Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was of Beauvais.
en: Just like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais.

raw: Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was of repute in Paris.
en: Like your father, he was well-known in Paris.

raw: I had the honour of knowing him there.
en: I had the honor of knowing him there.

raw: Our relations were business relations, but confidential.
en: Our relationship was professional, but very confidential.

raw: I was at that time in our French House, and had been--oh! twenty years.”
en: At that time, I was working in our French branch, and had been there for, oh, twenty years."

raw: “At that time--I may ask, at what time, sir?”
en: "At that time, may I ask, what time was that, sir?"

raw: “I speak, miss, of twenty years ago.
en: "I am speaking of twenty years ago, miss.

raw: He married--an English lady--and I was one of the trustees.
en: He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees of his estate.

raw: His affairs, like the affairs of many other French gentlemen and French families, were entirely in Tellson’s hands.
en: His financial affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen, were kept entirely in Tellson's hands.

raw: In a similar way I am, or I have been, trustee of one kind or other for scores of our customers.
en: In the same way, I have acted as a trustee in some form for dozens of our clients.

raw: These are mere business relations, miss; there is no friendship in them, no particular interest, nothing like sentiment.
en: These are purely business relationships, miss; there is no personal friendship in them, no special interest, nothing emotional.

raw: I have passed from one to another, in the course of my business life, just as I pass from one of our customers to another in the course of my business day; in short, I have no feelings; I am a mere machine.
en: I have moved from one client to another throughout my career just as I move from one account to another during my workday. In short, I have no feelings; I am just a machine.

raw: To go on--”
en: To continue, "

raw: “But this is my father’s story, sir; and I begin to think”--the curiously roughened forehead was very intent upon him--“that when I was left an orphan through my mother’s surviving my father only two years, it was you who brought me to England.
en: "But this is my father's story, sir." She paused. Her forehead wrinkled in that intense, searching way. "And I am starting to think that when I was left an orphan, because my mother only outlived my father by two years, it was you who brought me to England.

raw: I am almost sure it was you.”
en: I am almost sure it was you."

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry took the hesitating little hand that confidingly advanced to take his, and he put it with some ceremony to his lips.
en: Lorry took her small, hesitating hand as she reached out to him trustingly, and kissed it with polite ceremony.

raw: He then conducted the young lady straightway to her chair again, and, holding the chair-back with his left hand, and using his right by turns to rub his chin, pull his wig at the ears, or point what he said, stood looking down into her face while she sat looking up into his.
en: He then led the young lady back to her chair. He stood behind the chair, holding the back of it with his left hand. With his right hand he rubbed his chin, adjusted his wig, or gestured as he spoke. He stood looking down at her face. She sat looking up at him.

raw: “Miss Manette, it _was_ I.
en: "Miss Manette, it was me.

raw: And you will see how truly I spoke of myself just now, in saying I had no feelings, and that all the relations I hold with my fellow-creatures are mere business relations, when you reflect that I have never seen you since.
en: And you will see how true it is that I have no feelings, and that all my relationships are strictly professional, when you realize that I haven't seen you since that day.

raw: No; you have been the ward of Tellson’s House since, and I have been busy with the other business of Tellson’s House since.
en: No; you have been a ward of Tellson's Bank ever since, and I have been busy with other bank business.

raw: Feelings!
en: Feelings!

raw: I have no time for them, no chance of them.
en: I have no time for them, no opportunity for them.

raw: I pass my whole life, miss, in turning an immense pecuniary Mangle.”
en: I spend my whole life, miss, turning a giant money-grinding machine."

raw: After this odd description of his daily routine of employment, Mr.
en: After this strange description of his daily work, Mr.

raw: Lorry flattened his flaxen wig upon his head with both hands (which was most unnecessary, for nothing could be flatter than its shining surface was before), and resumed his former attitude.
en: Lorry flattened his light wig onto his head with both hands. It was completely unnecessary, nothing could possibly be flatter than it already was. Then he returned to his previous posture.

raw: “So far, miss (as you have remarked), this is the story of your regretted father.
en: "So far, miss, as you noted, this is the story of your late father.

raw: Now comes the difference.
en: Now comes the difference.

raw: If your father had not died when he did--Don’t be frightened!
en: If your father had not died when he did, don't be frightened!

raw: How you start!”
en: Why do you jump like that?"

raw: She did, indeed, start.
en: She did jump, startled.

raw: And she caught his wrist with both her hands.
en: And she grabbed his wrist with both hands.

raw: “Pray,” said Mr.
en: "Please," said Mr.

raw: “As I was saying; if Monsieur Manette had not died; if he had suddenly and silently disappeared; if he had been spirited away; if it had not been difficult to guess to what dreadful place, though no art could trace him; if he had an enemy in some compatriot who could exercise a privilege that I in my own time have known the boldest people afraid to speak of in a whisper, across the water there; for instance, the privilege of filling up blank forms for the consignment of any one to the oblivion of a prison for any length of time; if his wife had implored the king, the queen, the court, the clergy, for any tidings of him, and all quite in vain;--then the history of your father would have been the history of this unfortunate gentleman, the Doctor of Beauvais.”
en: "As I was saying: suppose Monsieur Manette did not die. Suppose he simply vanished one day, silently and without a trace. Suppose he was taken away. It would be easy enough to guess which terrible place he had been sent to, even if no one could prove it. Suppose he had an enemy, someone with the power to sign blank arrest warrants and lock anyone away in a silent prison forever. That power was so feared in France that even the bravest people refused to whisper about it. Suppose his wife went to the king, the queen, the court, and the church, begging for any news of her husband. All of that begging would come to nothing. If all of this were true, then the story of your father would be the story of this unfortunate gentleman, the Doctor of Beauvais."

en: When she died, brokenhearted, I believe, having never stopped searching for your father, she left you, at two years old, to grow up healthy, beautiful, and happy. She spared you the dark cloud of wondering whether your father died quickly in prison or wasted away there over many long years."
